name: Orujo
description: Galicia's pomace spirit, clear and fiery, and the base of the queimada ritual in which it is set alight in a clay bowl while someone recites a spell against witches. That part is not a tourist invention.
funFact: The queimada conxuro, the spell recited while the orujo burns, was written in the 1950s but draws on genuinely older Galician folk practice.

serve.how: Cool and neat after a meal, or as the herbal and cream versions that Galician bars keep alongside the clear one. For queimada it is burned with sugar, coffee beans and lemon peel in a clay bowl.

composition.summary: Grape pomace from Galician wine fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Skins, pips and stems, largely Albariño and Mencía

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper alquitara or pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; herbal and cream versions are infused after

composition.process: Traditional alquitaras are small enough that distilling was historically done village by village.

name: Pacharán
description: Navarrese sloes steeped in anise spirit until the liquid runs deep red, then sweetened. Softer than sloe gin and unmistakably aniseed, it is what northern Spain drinks when the meal is over.
funFact: Navarre protects it by denomination, requiring at least 125 grams of sloes per litre and a minimum steeping period before bottling.

serve.how: Over a couple of ice cubes, after dinner, which is how it is served in every bar in Navarre. It is sweet enough that ice is an improvement rather than a compromise.

composition.summary: Blackthorn sloes macerated in anise-flavoured spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Anisado, an aniseed-flavoured neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Wild or cultivated sloes, minimum 125g per litre

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for one to eight months

composition.process: The sloes must be steeped, never merely flavoured, and the colour comes entirely from the fruit skins.

name: Licor 43
description: Forty-three ingredients, vanilla and citrus loudest among them, in a bright yellow Spanish liqueur that tastes far more of custard than of anything herbal. Enormously popular in Spain and largely misunderstood elsewhere.
funFact: The company traces the recipe to a Carthaginian liqueur the Romans tried to ban, which is an excellent story and impossible to verify.

serve.how: Over ice with cold milk poured on top, which is the Barraquito or Leche y Licor 43 and by far the most common Spanish serve. Neat over ice also works, and it goes well into coffee.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit flavoured with citrus, vanilla and 43 botanicals.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: 43 ingredients: citrus fruits, vanilla, herbs and spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended, then sweetened

composition.process: Vanilla dominates so thoroughly that most tasters never register the other forty-two.

name: Anís
description: Spain's aniseed liqueur, made dulce or seco, and a fixture of village bars and grandmothers' cupboards alike. Anís del Mono has been sold in the same faceted, monkey-labelled bottle since 1870.
funFact: The monkey on the Anís del Mono label was drawn with Darwin's face, a joke about evolution that scandalised Catalonia in 1870.

serve.how: Seco neat and cold; dulce over ice or with a splash of water, which turns it cloudy. It is also drunk with coffee as a carajillo, and in some regions poured directly into it.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit distilled or macerated with green anise and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Green anise seed, sometimes star anise and fennel

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the seed, then sweetened to dulce or seco

composition.process: Anethole from the anise is what clouds the liquid when water is added, the same effect as in ouzo and pastis.

name: Hierbas
description: The Balearic herb liqueur, strongest in Ibiza and Mallorca, made by steeping local plants in anise spirit. Bottles often carry whole sprigs of rosemary, fennel and thyme still floating inside.
funFact: Ibicencan families each keep their own herb mix, and the island protects Hierbas Ibicencas under its own denomination.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass after eating, or over ice in summer. The dulce version is thick and sweet; the seca is drier and closer to a straight herbal anise.

composition.summary: Anise spirit macerated with Balearic herbs.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Anise-flavoured spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Rosemary, thyme, fennel, lemon verbena, juniper, orange leaf

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated; sprigs often left in the bottle

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 20–40% depending on style

composition.process: Leaving the herbs in means the liqueur keeps changing on the shelf, which producers treat as a feature.

name: Ron Miel
description: Canary Islands honey rum: local rum blended with palm or bee honey until it is thick, sweet and only about 20% alcohol. The archipelago's own category, and almost never found off the islands.
funFact: The Canaries grew sugar cane from the fifteenth century and supplied the cuttings that started the industry in the Caribbean.

serve.how: Chilled and neat in a small glass, or over ice. Canarians drink it after dinner and pour it over ice cream. It is sweet enough that anything more than a small measure becomes hard work.

composition.summary: Canary rum blended with honey and spice.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Rum distilled in the Canary Islands

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Bee honey or palm honey, vanilla, cinnamon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Blended after distillation

composition.process: Palm honey, made from boiled palm sap rather than by bees, gives the more traditional version its darker edge.

name: Aguardente Vínica
description: Portuguese wine brandy, and the spirit that stops port fermenting. Most of it never reaches a glass on its own, which is a shame, because the aged bottlings can stand comfortably beside a young cognac.
funFact: Port producers historically used a neutral grape spirit of exactly 77% to fortify their wine, a figure fixed by regulation for decades.

serve.how: Neat after dinner. Aged Portuguese brandies are usually softer and sweeter than French ones, so resist the urge to warm the glass; heat pushes them toward syrup.

composition.summary: Wine distilled and aged in oak in Portugal.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Portuguese wine, often from the Douro or Bairrada

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot or column still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Oak, from a few years to several decades

composition.process: The unaged, near-neutral version is what goes into port; the aged version is the drink.

name: Aguardente Bagaceira
description: Portugal's pomace brandy, the rougher country cousin of the wine brandy. Northern Portugal drinks it after coffee, poured straight into the cup once the coffee is finished, a habit called café com cheirinho.
funFact: Café com cheirinho translates as coffee with a little scent, which understates the quantity most people pour.

serve.glass: Small glass, or into the coffee cup
serve.how: A small measure after a meal, or the northern habit of swilling it around the empty espresso cup and drinking it from there. Aged versions in oak are smoother and worth seeking out.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and distilled after the press.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Skins, pips and stems from Portuguese winemaking

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Pot still, often in small rural distilleries

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Frequently unaged; velha versions are oak-rested

composition.process: Vinho verde country produces some of the sharpest and most aromatic examples.

name: Medronho
description: Distilled from the fruit of the strawberry tree, which grows wild across the Algarve and Alentejo hills and ripens a full year after it flowers. Genuinely difficult to make well and frequently made badly.
funFact: The medronho fruit ferments slightly on the tree, which is why deer and birds in the Algarve have a reputation for behaving oddly in autumn.

serve.how: Cool, neat, in a small pour after a meal. Honey-sweetened versions, melosa, are common in Algarve bars. The unadulterated version is the one to look for, and it should smell of the fruit rather than of alcohol.

composition.summary: Wild strawberry-tree fruit fermented and pot-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Arbutus unedo fruit, hand-picked from wild trees

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Small copper pot stills, often licensed to individual growers

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged

composition.process: The fruit is fragile and must be picked ripe and fermented quickly, which limits the scale of production.

name: Ginjinha
description: Sour cherry liqueur, drunk standing up in tiny Lisbon bars that sell almost nothing else. A shot costs small change, arrives with or without a cherry in it, and is finished on the pavement outside.
glassware: Small shot glass or chocolate cup
funFact: In Óbidos it is served in a small cup made of dark chocolate, which you drink from and then eat.

serve.glass: Small shot glass, or an edible chocolate cup
serve.how: One small glass, standing, com or sem — with or without the steeped cherry at the bottom. Always com, for the record. Room temperature is traditional and chilling it flattens the cinnamon.

composition.summary: Sour ginja cherries steeped in aguardente with sugar and cinnamon.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Aguardente or neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Ginja sour cherries, sugar, cinnamon, sometimes clove

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for several months

composition.process: Some producers crush a portion of the stones with the fruit, which is where the almond note comes from.

name: Licor Beirão
description: A seed and herb liqueur from the Beira region, made since 1929 and marketed for decades as the liqueur of Portugal, which it more or less is. Sweet, warmly spiced, and drunk at every temperature.
funFact: Its advertising is a national in-joke; the slogan O licor de Portugal has appeared on billboards positioned to be visible from motorway traffic jams for decades.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a shot glass, or long with tonic and lime as a caipirinha-style Beirão. Portuguese bars also pour it over ice with lemon in summer.

composition.summary: Seeds and herbs distilled in water and alcohol, then sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Cardamom, anise, eucalyptus, lavender, cinnamon, mint

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double-distilled with the botanicals, then sweetened

composition.process: The seeds come from several continents, and the exact blend has never been published.

name: Aguardente de Cana
description: Madeiran cane spirit, distilled from fresh juice rather than molasses, which technically makes it an agricole rum. It exists mainly to be turned into poncha, the island's honey-and-lemon cure-all.
funFact: Poncha is stirred with a caralhinho, a grooved wooden stick made for the purpose and found in every bar on the island.

serve.how: Rarely drunk neat. Mixed into poncha with lemon juice and honey and stirred hard with a wooden muddler until it emulsifies, then drunk immediately while still cloudy.

composition.summary: Fresh sugarcane juice fermented and distilled on Madeira.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Fresh-pressed Madeiran cane juice

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Column or pot still, unaged

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually none; some aged expressions exist

composition.process: Cane has been grown on Madeira since the fifteenth century, which predates the Caribbean industry entirely.

name: Italian Brandy
description: Wine brandy made across Italy, softer and sweeter than cognac, and long treated as a domestic staple rather than a luxury. Vecchia Romagna and Stravecchio Branca are the names most Italians grew up with.
funFact: Italy could not legally call it cognac after 1948, so producers coined arzente, a word Gabriele d'Annunzio invented, before settling on brandy.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or in coffee as a caffè corretto, which is what most of it is actually used for. Italian brandy tends to be sweeter than French, so it needs less warming.

composition.summary: Italian wine distilled and aged in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Trebbiano and other Italian white wine

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Continuous or pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Minimum one year, quality grades far longer, in Slavonian or Limousin oak

composition.process: Slavonian oak is more neutral than French, which keeps Italian brandy leaning fruity rather than woody.

name: Amaro
description: Not one drink but a whole Italian category: bittersweet herbal digestives, one for nearly every region, ranging from gentle and orange-scented to aggressively medicinal. Montenegro, Averna, Nonino and Braulio are all amari and none tastes like another.
funFact: Most amari began as monastic or pharmacy preparations, and several are still made to recipes written by nineteenth-century chemists.

serve.how: Neat after a meal at room temperature, which is how Italy drinks it. Lighter amari take ice and soda well; heavy ones do not. In cocktails they swap in for vermouth to add bitterness without more alcohol.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit or wine macerated with bitter herbs, roots and peel, then sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit, sometimes a wine base

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Gentian, cinchona, rhubarb, wormwood, citrus peel, spices

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated or infused, then sweetened and rested

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Varies; some rest in oak for years

composition.process: Bitterness comes from roots and barks, sweetness from sugar syrup, and the balance between them defines the house style.

name: Mirto
description: Sardinian myrtle liqueur, made from the berries for the dark red version and the leaves for the white. Every Sardinian household makes it, and every restaurant on the island pours it unasked at the end of a meal.
funFact: Myrtle grows wild across the Sardinian maquis, and the berries are picked between November and January when they are fully black.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a small chilled glass, after dinner. Warm mirto turns medicinal quickly. The red is sweeter and more common; the white, from the leaves, is drier and harder to find.

composition.summary: Wild myrtle berries or leaves macerated in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Myrtus communis berries (rosso) or leaves (bianco)

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for several weeks, then sweetened

composition.process: The berries are never crushed, only steeped, since crushing releases a harsh tannin.

name: Strega
description: Seventy herbs and saffron in a bright yellow liqueur from Benevento, a town with a long reputation for witchcraft. Strega means witch, and the branding has committed to it entirely for a hundred and sixty years.
funFact: Local legend holds that a couple who drink Strega together will be united forever, which the company has never once discouraged anyone from believing.

serve.how: Neat after dinner, or over ice in summer. It is also poured over gelato and used in Neapolitan baking, where it flavours the sponge in a great many cakes.

composition.summary: About seventy botanicals distilled, then coloured with saffron.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Around 70, including mint, fennel, juniper and Ceylon cinnamon

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Distilled with the botanicals, then sweetened

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Rested in oak vats before bottling

composition.process: The yellow is saffron and nothing else, which is why it is expensive to make.

name: Galliano
description: Vanilla and anise in a bottle so tall it does not fit on most shelves, named after an Italian war hero and built for the American market. Without it there is no Harvey Wallbanger, which may or may not be an argument in its favour.
funFact: The bottle shape is modelled on a Roman column, and its height was a deliberate bid for visibility on crowded back bars.

serve.temp: room temp or in a long drink
serve.glass: Cordial glass, or highball in a drink
serve.how: Neat in a small glass after dinner, or floated on top of a screwdriver to make a Harvey Wallbanger. The higher-strength L'Autentico is drier and better in cocktails than the standard bottling.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit infused with vanilla, anise and herbs, then sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Star anise, Mediterranean anise, vanilla, juniper, lavender, ginger

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Botanicals distilled separately, then blended with vanilla infusion

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 30% standard, 42.3% for L'Autentico

composition.process: Vanilla is added as an infusion after distillation, since distilling it would strip the character out.

name: Frangelico
description: Hazelnut liqueur from Piedmont, with cocoa and vanilla behind it, sold in a bottle shaped like a friar complete with a rope belt. The monastic story is decoration; the hazelnuts are real and local.
funFact: Piedmont's Tonda Gentile hazelnuts are the same variety that goes into the region's other famous product, and they are grown a short distance from where Nutella is made.

serve.how: Over one large cube, or neat at room temperature after dinner. It works well in coffee, and it is the standard nut liqueur in a Nutty Irishman or an espresso martini variant.

composition.summary: Toasted hazelnuts infused into neutral spirit with cocoa and vanilla.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Toasted Piedmont hazelnuts, cocoa, vanilla, coffee

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Nuts steeped, then the infusion distilled and blended

composition.process: Toasting before infusion is what turns the nut note from raw and green to roasted.

name: Tsipouro
description: Greek pomace spirit, made with or without anise depending on where you are standing. Thessaly and Epirus drink it unanised and cold with a table full of small plates, which is most of the point.
funFact: Monks on Mount Athos are credited with formalising the distillation in the fourteenth century, and monasteries there still produce it.

serve.how: Cold, in small glasses, alongside mezedes rather than after them. A tsipouradiko will keep bringing food with each round, which is the correct way to spend an afternoon in Volos.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and distilled, sometimes with anise.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Grape pomace from Greek winemaking

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, once or twice

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Usually unaged; oak-aged versions exist

composition.process: Adding anise is a regional choice rather than a rule, and northern Greece mostly leaves it out.

name: Tsikoudia
description: Crete's pomace spirit, always without anise, always poured at the end of a meal whether you asked for it or not. Cretans call it raki, which causes endless confusion with the Turkish drink it resembles not at all.
funFact: Refusing the complimentary tsikoudia at the end of a Cretan meal is close to a social offence, and it usually arrives with a plate of fruit.

serve.how: Cold, neat, in tiny glasses, poured for the whole table at once. It is a communal drink and drinking it alone is regarded as slightly odd. Rakomelo, warmed with honey and cinnamon, is the winter version.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and single-distilled on Crete.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Cretan grape pomace

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single distillation in a copper kazani

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 37–60%, village versions running higher

composition.process: Autumn distilling is a social event on Crete, with the still running all night and food cooked over the fire.

name: Mastiha
description: Made from the resin of mastic trees, which produce it only on the southern half of Chios and nowhere else on earth despite centuries of attempts to transplant them. Pine-like, faintly sweet, and completely distinctive.
funFact: Mastic is harvested by scoring the bark and letting the resin drip onto swept ground, a method unchanged since antiquity and protected by UNESCO.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in a small glass after dinner. It also works over ice with soda and a strip of lemon, and Greek bartenders use it in place of a herbal liqueur in gin drinks.

composition.summary: Mastic tree resin distilled or infused into spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit or tsipouro

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Mastiha resin from Pistacia lentiscus var. Chia

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Resin distilled or macerated, then sweetened

composition.process: The trees only weep usable mastic on Chios, an agricultural mystery nobody has fully explained.

name: Metaxa
description: Not quite a brandy: aged wine distillate blended with muscat wine and a botanical infusion, which puts it in a category of one. Greece's best-known spirit abroad, and consistently mislabelled as brandy on every back bar.
funFact: Spyros Metaxas created it in 1888, and the star rating on the label denotes years of ageing, running from three stars up to the Private Reserve.

serve.glass: Snifter, or rocks glass with a large cube
serve.how: Neat at room temperature for the older expressions; the three and five star take ice and tonic well. Greeks also drink it long with cola, which the higher stars do not deserve.

composition.summary: Aged wine distillate blended with muscat wine and rose petal infusion.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Savatiano, Sultanina and Black Corinth wine distillate

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Muscat wine from Samos plus a botanical infusion including rose petals

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Double-distilled, aged, then blended

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Three to thirty years in French Limousin oak

composition.process: The muscat wine is added after ageing, which is why it reads sweeter and more floral than any true brandy.

name: Kumquat Liqueur
description: Corfu's speciality, made from a fruit the British introduced to the island in the nineteenth century and which took to it completely. Bright orange, sweet, and sold in every shop on the island.
funFact: Kumquats reached Corfu with British botanists during the protectorate years, and the island now grows more of them than anywhere else in Europe.

serve.how: Cold and neat after a meal, or over ice with soda in summer. The clear version is distilled and drier; the orange one is a sweeter maceration and the one most visitors take home.

composition.summary: Corfiot kumquats macerated or distilled into spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Whole Corfu kumquats, skin and all

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for the orange version, distilled for the clear

composition.process: The peel is where nearly all the flavour lives, which is why the fruit goes in whole.

name: Zivania
description: Cypriot pomace and wine spirit, clear, unaged and traditionally very strong. Protected by the EU since 2004, and used on the island as a disinfectant, a chest rub and a drink, in roughly that order of frequency.
funFact: Village zivania has historically been distilled well above bottling strength, and it is still used in Cypriot households to treat wounds and joint pain.

serve.how: Straight from the freezer in small glasses with meze. Cypriots serve it with dried fruit and nuts through winter. The commercial bottlings sit around 45%; the village stuff does not, and should be approached carefully.

composition.summary: Grape pomace and local wine distilled together.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pomace of Xynisteri and Mavro grapes, plus dry wine

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still

components.label: Aging
components.detail: None; it must be colourless

components.label: Strength
components.detail: 45% commercially, far higher in villages

composition.process: Blending wine back into the pomace before distilling is what separates zivania from a straight pomace brandy.

name: Filfar
description: A Cypriot orange liqueur whose recipe is claimed to be Venetian and centuries old, made from local bitter oranges and spice. Sweet, thick and unmistakably island-made.
funFact: The recipe is said to have been found in a Venetian manuscript on Cyprus, though the modern product dates from the 1940s.

serve.glass: Small cordial glass or rocks glass
serve.how: Cold and neat, or over ice with soda. It substitutes for triple sec in a Margarita and brings more spice than the French orange liqueurs do.

composition.summary: Cypriot oranges and spices macerated in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Cypriot bitter orange peel, cinnamon, clove and herbs

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated and blended

composition.process: Local bitter oranges give more peel oil and less sugar than sweet varieties would.

name: Bajtra
description: Prickly pear liqueur from Malta, made from a cactus that arrived as a colonial import and has since taken over every rubble wall on the islands. Deep pink, faintly floral, and unlike anything else in the Mediterranean.
funFact: Prickly pear hedges were planted across Malta as field boundaries, and the fruit was for centuries a peasant food rather than a luxury.

serve.how: Straight from the fridge in a small glass after dinner. It is also good over ice with prosecco on top, and Maltese bars use it to colour and sweeten summer spritzes.

composition.summary: Prickly pear fruit macerated in spirit and sweetened.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Neutral spirit

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Opuntia ficus-indica fruit, hand-harvested

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated, strained and sweetened

composition.process: The fruit is covered in fine barbed spines, so harvesting is done at dawn while dew holds them down.
